utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Prosecution would wish to raise a preliminary matter. Can we do it in open session, Mr. Groome, or should we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would request private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. How are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of today I would like to again remind you since we are both speaking English that we will need to pause between question and answer and that way everyone who is following our work today can do their work. Is that understood again today, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to take up and discuss your actual deployment to the BH command as part of UNPROFOR, and I am going to start off with some general questions first. During the entirety of your tenure as the BH commander, did you ever threaten to use deadly force by way of air strikes or artillery strikes against either the BiH forces, that is the Bosnian Muslim forces, or the Bosnian Croat armed forces; and, if so, how many times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't think of a particular incident when I made such a threat, and I'm not sure that other than in the general measures of the safe areas and no-fly zone, and so forth, that the matter was -- that I talked about such threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the sake of completeness, how about the army of the Republic of Croatia? During the entirety of your tenure as the BH commander, do you recall ever having to threaten to use deadly force by way of air strikes or artillery against this armed formation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the record, will you agree or did you have knowledge that the Croatian army had troops which had crossed into the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, crossed the international boundary between them and were situated in and engaging in combat operations on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina during your tenure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During it or was there a -- are you giving me a time or at any time?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I was going to ask you -- let's go with more general, any time. Are you aware of any such operations by --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Towards the end of the year of 1995, yes, there were Croatian army forces in the western areas of Bosnia, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I to take then from your testimony that you are unaware of any actions of the Croatian regular army within Bosnia and Herzegovina, apart from what you have said towards the end of the year 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember any other case, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then if we can focus on the time-period towards the end of the year of 1995. At that time did UNPROFOR, either yourself or any other organs of UNPROFOR, take any measures to protest these actions in relation to the Croatian regular army being both within Bosnia-Herzegovina and engaging in these actions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall anyone. I didn't. And I can't recall if any other -- the people in Zagreb or anyone did it. It would be more likely to have happened from Zagreb than from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say it would have been more likely to have happened from Zagreb than from Sarajevo. What about in the instance where Croatian regular army troops were attacking Bosnian Serb villages within your zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I don't recall that that was happening except at the very end of that period, and Zagreb -- the UN headquarters in Zagreb was clearly the one collocated with the capital -- in the capital of Croatia and it would have been where any political action, such as a protest, would have taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, if during your tenure, the Bosnian Serb side had complained to you of military actions being undertaken by the regular army of Croatian forces on the territory within your zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time we are talking about, the back end of 1995, no such complaint was made to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And just to finish off the statistics -- or strike that. Did you have occasion to hear or have information of any either allegations or confirmed incidents where the Croats had fired artillery shells into the city of Sarajevo during the course of your tenure as BH commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think there is an artillery piece in existence that could range Sarajevo from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I misspoke with my question. I meant to say the Bosnian Croats located within the territory of the former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did you have any occasion to have information that these forces had fired artillery shells into Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have no information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just get clarity, Mr. Ivetic. When you say Bosnian Croats, are these Bosnian citizens of Croatian origin?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I believe so. I was -- perhaps should have made reference to the HVO, the Croat Defence Union, which was an armed formation on the territory of the former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And perhaps I should ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Having this clarification, does that change your answer in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. I understood you to be referring to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at your written statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that would be P785 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe you still have your hard copy in front of you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to focus on paragraph number 12 to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which is to be found at page 4 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S versions in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, I would like to ask you to further discuss the mandate of UNPROFOR during the time of your deployment as BH commander. And here in your statement it says: "Our rules of engagement were wholly reactive. The UN initiated nothing in terms of the use of force. We were reacting to a situation in which force was being used. If force was used, under the rules of engagement we could respond in self-defence." And I want to ask you, sir, these rules of engagement that you have identified here, did they stay in place during the entirety of your tenure as BH commander or do you believe that they changed at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The formal rules of engagement document existed throughout my time in -- in command. The -- I can't recall whether these were amended at any stage. In the -- during that year, the document was -- I think it was amended, but I cannot recall when or at what stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you could assist us by identifying this document, by telling us which document you refer to? As in, who gave you this document, who drafted it, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a United Nations document. I can't -- it would have been a part of the military orders of the force which spelt out the rules of engagement. These were -- came down the chain of command from New York. They stipulated the circumstances of when weapons and what weapons could be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, these rules of engagement which you have summarised in your evidence in this paragraph and I supposed sourced from this document that you have now identified for us, did these apply to the role of UNPROFOR in a peacekeeping nature or did they also apply to UNPROFOR in the role of a peacemaker?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you would have to talk to those who drafted them. I -- they applied in -- they were to apply in those circumstances. I don't know what the drafters thought the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, what did you as a commander who was expected to apply within and abide by these rules, how did you understand them to apply to the situation that you were on the ground looking at? Were they to apply in situations of -- as a role of peacekeeper as well as a peacemaker?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I've said in that -- in my statement they were reactive. You were there to -- you could use force in self-defence. Now we are talking about it, I seem to remember that later in the year the orders were changed to the extent that force could be used to fulfil the mandate. But again, I'd need to see some documents to be sure of this -- that -- when that happened and if it actually happened or it was just my memory of a discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir, if the rules of engagement that were provided for you by the UNPROFOR chain of command dealt with a concept called "legitimate defence"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me see if I can refresh your recollection or perhaps we are talking about two different things. There was another UNPROFOR officer, whose name I will not give because of -- the identity is to be protected,

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, irrespective of the -- of the connotation of a legitimate defence or not, does this situation that this officer spoke of ring a bell as -- with you as to the procedures that were in place and the rules of engagement that you were expected to operate under?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It doesn't ring any bells, no. I think he is trying to explain the basis of self-defence. If you are directly threatened or attack you may respond, and that was the basis of the rules of engagement and that was the -- what I mean about them being wholly reactive.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for purposes of clarifying your answer, when you say "if you are directly threatened," the "you" in that instance would be UNPROFOR; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is the individual in the -- in the -- the rules of engagement are for the individual in the -- did not the -- it is not for the force of the whole. It is for the individual in that particular set of circumstances. No, the individual might be a commander of a group of people in that situation but it's not the force as a whole, as those types of orders are written.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall or do you know, upon assuming your position at BH command, whether you were advised if that mission was operating under chapters 6, 7, or 8 of the UN charter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew which it was at the time, and I think though it's -- it was -- heavens, I'd have to -- wait a minute. Can you remind me which is -- which of -- 6, of 6 and 7?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe it was probably under 7 but I've heard other witnesses say 6. That's why I was hoping you could assist us. I don't want to direct your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see. Which -- all right. I'd have to go and read this to be absolutely sure, but from memory --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic will help you by just giving the titles of chapter 6, 7, and 8. Isn't it, Mr. Ivetic, so that the witness has the guidance he needs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the sort of thing I am looking for, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even Mr. Ivetic has to consult a piece of paper for that so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can refresh your recollection, sir, under my understanding chapter 6 is entitled: "Specific Settlement of Disputes." And chapter 7 is entitled: "Action with Respect to Threats to the Peace, Breaches of the Peace and Acts of Aggression."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- now I've heard those descriptions, we were operating under 7 for the resolutions that -- the more recent of the resolutions. I think the very early resolutions that led to the deployment into the Balkans and into Bosnia specifically were under chapter 6, and subsequently they were under chapter 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I am looking at the clock. We'll soon take a break. But there is one matter which I would like to briefly put on the record. When you asked about legitimate defence and when the witness answered questions in that respect, he referred to being attacked or being under threat. Now, comparing the answer of this witness with what the previous witness you referred to said, is that he seemed to emphasise very much that there should be a smoking gun. You could not react up till the moment that, to say it short, you had been fired at. So where Mr. Smith referred to -- that he thought that it was about self-defence, what that witness said, there is a clear distinction that Mr. Smith included a situation of threat which does not yet require a gun being fired. I just would like to put this on the record because nothing further was asked about it. Mr. Smith, when you more or less qualified the evidence of the other witness I think you may have missed an important difference between what you said and what he appeared to have said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which I've just explained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take -- Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a matter in private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will -- do we need -- could the witness already take his break?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Smith, you are invited to follow the usher. We would like to see you back in a little bit over 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before taking the break we will turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to next take a look at something you said in the Perisic proceedings and ask you to provide further details on the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to call up 1D00594 in e-court, and I would like to call up page 48 of the same, which should correlate to transcript page 6299 of that Perisic transcript. And if we could focus in on line 17 and onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you could follow along with me, sir, I will read into the record this selection: "Q. Okay. Part of what I'm trying to understand here is the function of UNPROFOR. We have heard testimony that UNPROFOR's role was that of a peacekeeper, which you have rejected. "So I'm trying to get a sense of how you would characterise UNPROFOR's presence in Bosnia-Herzegovina, at least at the time that you were there. "A. I rejected the title of peacekeeper on what you might think rather narrow grounds, that there wasn't a peace to keep. And much of the concept of being a peacekeeper, particularly at the time and in the United Nations, was that you were, as it were, standing between two people who were agreed, given your presentation, to remain at peace. Perhaps an example would be Cyprus and the UN deployment there for some decades. "Q. That certainly wasn't the case that you were dealing with. "A. Exactly. And that is why I said we weren't peacekeepers. However, there is a very large number of people at the time in particular who understood what we were doing and why they had sent us there, and so forth, to be more in that example, the spirit, if you like, that you're not involved in the fighting as much. You're there to assist and ameliorate the condition of refugees and so on and so forth." First of all, sir, can you -- or do you stand by this selection of your prior testimony from the Perisic case as being accurate and truthful as to these matters that were discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I recognise this -- this discussion. I'd like to see it, the beginnings of it a bit more, and see where it goes to understand it, remember it fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can go back to the prior page and to the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You don't have to read it to the Court. It's just for me to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct. I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And now to the follow-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can have the next page and the selection after line 11 and onwards so the witness can review the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could have the next page for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you now in a position --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you now in a position, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I now recall the thing more clearly, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now can you answer my question as to if you can confirm --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps you could repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Of course. Can you confirm for me, sir, if you stand by this selection that we have read as being truthful and accurately depicting your testimony as to these questions that were raised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now as a follow-up question: Is it your position that within the role of UNPROFOR at the time that you were BH commander, that the UNPROFOR in Bosnia was never a peacekeeper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd go back to the testimony in the case you've put in front of me. There I am trying to explain that there were many people who thought we were doing such a thing and couched their expectations and instructions to us, and so forth, accordingly. I'm making that same point again, if you want me to, that in a narrow sense you cannot be a peacekeeper if there isn't an agreement to make peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you've indicated that these people were couching their expectations and instructions to you. First of all, can you identify who are "these people" that you are referring to? In --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- general terms --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- I'm sorry, I was connecting the two statements. This is the basis -- largely the basis upon which the United Nations force had been deployed by Security Council and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so by "these people," are you referring to the Security Council and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And what was your understanding of the mandate that the Security Council, and so forth, had given to you and to the UNPROFOR mission in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I say in my statement, that it was to protect and ensure the delivery of humanitarian aid and subsequently to carry out the instructions based on -- from the Security Council based on the decisions about the exclusion zones and the safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to now deal with -- with you -- with the -- for purposes of the record, the remainder of this page, beginning at line 12 onward. And I'll read for you: "Q. I understand what you said, and perhaps you can be of some assistance here, and this may be because I'm naive, but I've heard there is a distinction between being a peacekeeper and being a peacemaker. And by that I mean, when one has the mandate of being a peacekeeper [sic], then they can engage in active behaviours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are reading peacekeeper where it says peacemaker, Mr. -- and since you are [overlapping speakers] difference between the two is relevant here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, for catching that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will begin again then from line -- the end of line 14: "... and by that I mean, when one has the mandate of being a peacemaker, then they can engage in active behaviours, such as offensives or bombings in order to achieve an objective which is distinct from that of being a peacekeeper. "A. I'd -- you may not -- I don't want to connect -- I don't agree with your direct connection of offensives or bombings and being a peacemaker. They are not necessarily a connection to be made there. "Q. Do you see a distinction between the function of peacekeeping and peacemaking? "A. Clearly, if you have made -- if you had been party to making a peace, then you might, indeed, find yourself being party to keeping it. So ... "Q. With regard to making the peace, what different activities would exist, if any, in your mind? And I'm speaking militarily. "A. If -- if you -- if a political entity wishes to use its military to create a condition of peace, then it can be done. But in doing that, you have to decide what it is you want your military to do." And now with respect to this selection, sir, do you stand behind this testimony as being truthful and accurate as to this topic that is discussed therein?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the sake of completeness, let's just finish lines 9 through 17 as well: "Q. With regard to UNPROFOR's presence was - in your mind -- in your mind in understanding - the United Nations's wish that the military be used to create a condition of peace, as you have just stated? "A. No. Our military actions were all couched in the understanding that they were there for self-defence, and then a bit later on, defence increasing defence, if you like, of refugees and so forth within the safe areas. "Q. And that was the function of UNPROFOR? "A. Correct." And now, sir, with respect to these items from line 9 through 17 of this page of the Perisic transcript, do you affirm and stand behind this testimony as truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, sir, can you explain for us what it was that you meant when you were utilising the terminology "defence increasing defence"? Are you trying to say that this was an extension of self-defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the defence, as I go on to say in that sentence, of the people within the safe areas, and that we now had with the safe area regime and then the seclusion zones the -- this was a -- the -- the requirement was placed upon UNPROFOR to become part of the safe area and exclusion zone process - if that's quite the right word for it, I'm not sure - but the process would end ultimately if these regimes were not respected with the calling upon and activating the threat of NATO air power being used against whomsoever violated those regimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I take it from your answer, sir - and please correct me if I'm wrong - that the threats of action again violators of the regime within the safe areas would apply equally to any side in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the -- the -- as I recall the papers, the resolutions, and so forth, that were the basis on which these -- this regime was established, yes, it applied to anybody who violated them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for instance, then, sir, when the BiH Muslim forces engaged in offensive actions from within either the enclaves or Sarajevo, in your mind, was this a violation of the regime that required yourself and/or NATO to threaten or use air strikes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I consulted with my colleagues. All these questions on the abstract level are not what we -- what assists this Chamber very much. So if you have -- if you want to deal with that, do it, please, on the factual level rather than on an abstract level. The "ifs" and the "ands" are too numerous at this moment. And that may have been true for the previous testimony as well, but the Chamber would like to hear questions and answers that assist it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask you for a specific question, sir, to be clear. Am I understanding the testimony then as being: In addition to self-defence that there was a second ground for air strikes which was to enforce the exclusion and demilitarisation zones in Sarajevo and the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is not a concrete question either, Mr. Ivetic. It is again on the abstract level. "The second ground for air strikes," which air strike? When? How? What?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am referring to the witness's testimony, that there was two rationales for air strikes. One, self-defence; and one which was defence, as he stated it [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was not without reason that I said that the previous testimony may have suffered from the same and that the Chamber wants to avoid at least that it happens in this case as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to the air strikes which you recommended against the Serb side, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And to begin I'd like to look at 1D00596, page 30 of that in e-court which would correlate to page 11506 of the Karadzic transcript. And I'd look at lines 9 through 15 of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "Q. Thank you, but at the time you already knew -- or actually, you took part in making the plans for using force against the Army of Republika Srpska, and what was being awaited was just a good opportunity; right? "A. It wasn't a question of waiting for the opportunity. It was the question of waiting for the event to occur. We had to have an attack on a safe area first."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you tell me when we are talking about? Where are we in the chronology of that year?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you can look on the page -- if I can direct your attention to the first line, it appears we are talking of the 25th of August. That was the questions leading up to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So I believe we are talking about the Markale -- leading up to the end of the year, the second air strikes that were initiated. Is that -- is my recollection accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm now -- I'm now, as it were, in that month.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you then, sir, can you confirm that your statements made in response to Mr. Karadzic's questions are truthful and accurate as to that question that was posed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in reference to this time-period and that answer, am I correct that you did not have in mind a particular event that could be comitted by the other parties to the conflict, that is the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims, which would trigger air strikes, but you did have an event in mind which would trigger air strikes against the Serbs? Am I understanding your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't think you are understanding it correctly. My -- what I'm answering is a specific question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I understanding your answer to that question to be that you were waiting for a particular incident on the part of the Bosnian Serbs to bomb the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is in the context after the London Conference where the nature of the safe areas and the safe area regime has been explicitly stated again as a threat, this time specifically to the Republika Srpska. The -- and it applies to all the safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But it only applies to one party to the conflict; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the London Conference, that -- the case, if the Bosnian Serbs attacked a safe area, then this -- the threat placed in front of the Bosnian Serbs would be enacted. That was a decision of the London Conference and that's the basis, I think, of the quote that I -- being taken out of the book I wrote, that is the basis of this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the record, sir, at the time that the incident occurred in Markale in August of 1995, General Janvier was out of the zone, and thus the key to turn for commencement of NATO strikes was in your hands; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can go backwards in time and focus on the beginning of May, at that time you had also wanted to start air attacks against the Serbs, but that decision was countermanded by UN HQ in Zagreb by General Janvier; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that he was the one countermanding it. It was certainly not agreed with by that headquarters. I can't -- I'd have to refresh my memory from my statement as to the exact details of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe that's at paragraph 103 of your statement, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that, for purposes of the rest of us, is page 25 and 26 of the English version in e-court; and it should be page, I believe, page 22 and page 23 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I have some further documents that might assist you as well. First of all, if we can focus on this instance where the strikes were countermanded, am I correct that the flare point for this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I just respond. They weren't countermanded. It wasn't mine to make the decision. I requested it and it was denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. I apologise for my lax terminology. The flare point or issue that started off the request for the strikes on this occasion was a shell that had struck both military and civilian targets in front of a tunnel in Butmir, a suburb of Sarajevo, killing nine persons and wounding 15, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether those -- let me look at it. Whether that's the absolute numbers in my statement, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, that's not what the statement of the witness says. The witness, at paragraph 103 which you referred us to, clearly distinguishes between the shelling of the people in uniform and shelling of civilians later on the 7th and 8th. I think that's an embellishment of the statement of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe I said the flare point when he started -- I believe in the statement he said he decided --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not the flare point.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He says that during that day, I have to say I'm talking about the mortars that killed 11 people in Butmir entrance to the tunnel, some of whom were in uniform. And then he goes on to say that: "During that day, pressure for air strikes grew, but on a balance I decided not to request a strike at that time because I considered this was part of the fighting between two sides and there were people in uniform involved." And something else happens on the night of the 7th and 8th May, which was the shelling of civilians. That's when you request.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could return to the prior incident in Butmir. First of all, the Butmir tunnel, are we talking about the tunnel under the airport being used by the ABiH forces to supply their city and their forces within the city with various items, including munitions, weapons, and personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what came down the tunnel but that was where the tunnel came out in -- under the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In your -- your -- in paragraph 103, the selection that the Honourable Judge Moloto had read for us, you indicated that pressure was increasing. Could you identify for us from where. What parties were you receiving pressure to engage in bombing activities against the VRS at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall the -- specifically, but amongst others there would be people ringing up from embassies asking what was happening. And -- and whether this was an incident that would warrant such activity. The Bosnian government would have had a -- a -- would be making suggestions and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can now take a look at 1D00578 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for that, sir, I can tell you that it is an outgoing code cable from Akashi to Annan, dated 8th May, 1995, with the subject line of "Air strikes." And I would direct you first to the first page and the selection that states there: "As requested, please find attached the request from Sarajevo. General Smith has just informed me that he regrets having made the request. The official copies will be sent tomorrow through the normal channels." The question I have for you, sir, is can you enlighten us as to what this phrase means? What kind of regrets did you convey to the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall regretting making the request. I might have -- I'm trying to think why I might have said I regretted it. It may have been that the -- that it was very late in the day and that we had not requested anything and said we weren't going to for the reasons I put in my statement that I decided that this was part of the fighting. And then there was this apparent change of mind. It may have been that that is what he -- I was saying I'm sorry that I had changed my mind, rather than that I had informed -- that I'd made the request at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could have the assistance of the court personnel to turn to the fourth page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And here, sir, we have a section entitled: "Collateral Damage." And I'd like to ask you, we see here in under civilian buildings that for 1 and 2 there are civilian inhabited instructions 200 metres from 1 and 2. Are 1 and 2 projected targets or targets that you supplied for the air strikes, proposed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall. I'd have to have a bigger file than you're showing me here to give you -- to have an idea of what those are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at -- if we can look at page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does that refresh your recollection of whether 1, 2, and 3 are targets that you proposed for this set of air strikes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see that 1, 2, and 3 are listed as proposed targets. I do not recall the -- whether that is actually the ones that we did and so forth. That's too long ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking, sir, is from these documents are these the ones that were proposed, not the ones that were actually hit. [Overlapping speakers] air strikes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, clearly, 1, 2, and 3 of paragraph 2 refers to the 1, 2, and 3s of the first page you showed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then can we return to page 4 so I can have a follow-up. Does this selection under "Collateral Damage" accurately reflect your assessment as to the potential for collateral damage from these air strikes that you sought?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose it did at the time. Yup.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it your position that striking military targets located within 200 metres of civilian inhabited structures was appropriate or acceptable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was -- it was at that time and the -- and if you look at my recommendation I want them recce'd in order to confirm their current situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to target number 3, am I correct that they had absolutely no information as to the location of potential civilians near that -- that target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. And again, I'd point out I'm asking for reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to the second-to-last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We see here that it's not authorised, and it's, I believe, signed by General Janvier. Does that refresh your recollection as to who denied your request for the air strikes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I say I don't recall. And now you've shown me that. It's not a recollection. Now I see that he's signed the document. I don't suppose I ever saw this document returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you ever given a reason by your superiors in UNPROFOR as to why these particular air strikes you sought in the beginning of May 1995 were denied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall a specific set of reasons, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can ask for this document to be admitted as the next available Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 1D578 shall be assigned Exhibit D135.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D135 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we can return to events leading up to Markale 2 in August of 1995, and I'd like to first discuss with you 65 ter 25919, which is your book, "The Utility of Force," and I'd like to turn to page 186 in e-court which should correlate to page 364 in that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again we're looking for page 186 in e-court which should be page 364 -- there we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at the top of the page is what I'm focussing on, sir. And it reads as follows: "The RRF continued to deploy and, after considerable obstructions placed by the Croats and Bosniaks had been overcome, we had an artillery group on Mount Igman overlooking Sarajevo. The French were still adamant that their artillery units were there to support the French units. Since the French were all in Sarajevo and I had only enough helicopters to lift elsewhere from the British artillery regiment, one six-gun battery and supply it with ammunition, the place I could have a fight and employ the greatest fire-power was in the Sarajevo area. So in the end, the decision taken at the London Conference came down to this: If I was to use the forces available to me, NATO and the RRF, to best effect, I had to seize the first opportunity presented by an attack on Sarajevo and, if at all possible, ignore attacks on the other safe areas. Having done the planning with NATO, I was aware there were only so many targets suitable for air strikes. The more we could mix the mode of attack - air, artillery, and the battle groups - the greater our options and effect; by a wide margin this was achieved best around Sarajevo." And I want to ask you, first of all, RRF is referring to the Rapid Reaction Force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I to understand that the decision to attack just the Bosnian Serbs around Sarajevo had been made at the time of the London Conference well in advance of any shelling incidents in August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you can't understand that. That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then when you say here that "the decision taken at the London Conference came down to this," what decision are you referring to then, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the risk of reading you the whole book, the London Conference lays down that any attack by the Bosnian Serbs on any safe area would be met by air attacks. Furthermore, the authority to call these air attacks in was removed from the Secretary General who was holding it at the time -- Secretary General of the UN who was holding it at the time and given to the commander of UNPROFOR -- or, I'm sorry, the force commander, General Janvier, and the NATO commander, the NATO commander in Naples.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I say, this required an attack before this threat would be initiated or put into effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so, again, I ask you my original question, which was: And the decision to attack just the Bosnian Serbs had been made at the time of the London Conference; that is to say, they excluded the possibility of attacks on any of the other warring factions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That wasn't your question. Your question included Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here you state that you were planning with NATO -- having done the planning with NATO. At this time were you operating as a UN officer or as a NATO officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the commander UNPROFOR. I was a UN officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And my question to you was: At this time were you operating as a UN officer or as a NATO officer? Please answer the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, he has answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, did I understand your answer well that when you were asked whether you were operating as a NATO officer or as a UN officer that when you said, "I was the commander of UNPROFOR," I understood that to be: I acted as such?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the common --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- understanding of this language. Mr. Ivetic, even if you have a different understanding, and even if you want to make that clear, then the tone you used is not the appropriate one. You could have asked: Do I have to understand your question -- your answer to be A or B. We take a break after the witness has left the courtroom and has followed the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, the Rapid Reaction Force that we just discussed, when it engaged in strikes against the Serbs in August and September of 1995, was it under your direct command and apart from the NATO chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then am I also correct then that in that time-period when NATO planes were striking at the Serbs and the RRF artillery under your command was striking the Serbs, that the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat forces a couple days later also initiated an offensive also against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, was that a question or a statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was a question. Am I correct that in the time-period when NATO planes were striking at the Serbs and the RRF artillery under your command are striking the Serbs, that the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats a couple of days later initiated an offensive also against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that at that time also the BiH Muslim forces actually identified specific Serb targets for the NATO air strikes to hit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't think they did do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to take a moment to look at document 1D00584.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for that, sir, it's a letter dated the 4th of September, 1995, from General Delic of the ABiH, directed to you, sir, General Smith. And can we look at the top of the document where it says that the recipient of the document. Would you agree that that would appear to be addressed to yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the last page of the document, does it appear to have originated from the General Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can return to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that the items identified in these pages are being asked by General Delic of you to be sent to NATO for their action against these identified Bosnian Serbs targets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't see any marking that I ever received this document or it was processed in my headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you a more general question: Do you receive -- do you recall receiving any similar documents of this nature from the ABiH during the time-period of the bombing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I said I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know or can you tell if any of the identified targets listed in this document originating from the ABiH were actually targeted by either the RRF or the NATO forces engaging the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you consider the ABiH to be your allies or on the same side as the RRF and the NATO forces during the duration of these air strikes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't, and I made a specific representation to the Bosnians to make it clear that I didn't expect them to take advantage of this situation right at the beginning of starting those air strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that they did take an advantage launching an offensive using heavy weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't do that around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly pause between questions and answers. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were the actions of the BiH side in violation of the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it had been existent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the actions of the ABiH warrant warnings of use of force against them for violation of the various agreements that were on the ground? And when I say the actions of the ABiH, I mean the counter-offensive, including the use of heavy weapons, which was initiated against the Bosnian Serbs at the same time that the NATO and RRF forces were also striking at the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, they didn't do that around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did your mandate extend only to Sarajevo or did you cover the entirety of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. But Sarajevo was a safe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I wish to tender this document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Prosecution objects, Your Honour. It's being tendered to suggest that this request was made to General Smith. This document was recovered from ABiH, and there is no evidence that I'm aware of that it ever made it to UNPROFOR, so on that basis we do object to its admission for the purpose it's being admitted for at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know yet what the purposes are. The witness has said that he's not aware that it ever reached him. Would you just tender it in order to demonstrate that it existed, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. Correct, Your Honours, and to give a bases to the questions that I asked and the answers that the gentleman made as to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection for that limited purpose, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 1D584 shall be assigned Exhibit D136.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, now I want to take a step back to take a closer look at the incident, the Markale incident, in August of 1995 which precipitated all these actions at the end of August and beginning of September. At paragraph 198 and onwards in your written statement, which is P785, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for those following it's page 50 in e-court in the English and page 39 in the B/C/S where this discussion begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 198, you identify that there had been a pattern of random shelling of a few rounds a day by the Serbs. And I'd like to ask you, would you agree with me that you have left out from your analysis the fact that the BiH government or Muslim forces had also engaged in a random shelling of a few rounds a day during this same time-period according to the UNMO records?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't left it out of an analysis. I might not have put it in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you help me understand your answer. Were you aware of the fact that the BiH government or Muslim forces had also engaged in the random shelling of a few rounds a day during this same time-period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I probably was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If -- if we could focus for a moment on a document that you handled in direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up Exhibit P797. And again, this is the final and comprehensive report, at least that's how it's presented on the cover page of this document, prepared by your MA, Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to focus for the moment on the first page. And the section 2 or item number 2 on the first page, wherein Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter states: "We must continue to be cautious about revealing our evidence and data to public scrutiny." First of all, did you, sir, order such precautions or did Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter come up with them of his own accord?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am quite happy to take responsibility for that statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you explain for us, sir, why it was that your command was not desirous to have the conclusions and investigations subjected to public scrutiny?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will read you what the rest of that paragraph said: "We reaffirm that we have nothing to hide, but by declaring our information we risk entering an expert argument which alleges," there should have been a "to" there, I think, "which led to a judgement. Other so-called experts have been and will continue to be selective in what evidence they choose to consider and adduce to support their judgements."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have faith in the findings and the methods used to reach the conclusions presented in this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you identify here other so-called experts have been and will continue to be selected. To whom are you referring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There had been one case in particular where a -- the deputy commander of sector Sarajevo, I think it was, had given a press interview in which he'd explained his understanding of what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could stay within the confines of this report now, this comprehensive report, one thing that struck me as odd, sir, is that it lacks items that I had become familiar with from other similar investigations or crater analyses, such as: First, a description of the crater site, photographs of the ordinance remnants, especially the tail fin, a photo or drawing of the crater itself, notations as to temperature and wind conditions, and a description of the precise technique used to determine the bearing measurements. Can you explain for me, sir, why this comprehensive report lacks such rudimentary features?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My suspicion is that they wouldn't have gone on a fax machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that the factors that I have recounted indeed are what you would expect to be found in a properly done crater analysis report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a properly done crater analysis report, and I am satisfied with its -- with the investigations conducted by my teams on the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I wish to turn to the sixth page in English in the document and the sixth page in the B/C/S. And this will correlate to what was identified, I believe, as annex A of the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, sir, do you recall Lieutenant-Colonel Mougey and what unit or structure he was operating under at the time of this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a French officer, if I recall correct, in sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we look at the last paragraph of this one page, this annex A, can you focus on the description of the munition as being unmarked and unpainted. And if I'm reading this correctly, we are talking about the tail fin of the mortar shell, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What he states in that paragraph is the munition is of a Serb manufacturer, being unmarked and unpainted with a brush steel finish, which matches current Bosno-Serb war design.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And can we look at the paragraph before that, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does the reference there relate to the examination of a tail fin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would that be "this munition" referred to in the paragraph that you just recited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here it is stating that this is -- what he says is the munition. We might deduce - but I didn't write the report - that what he meant from looking at the tail fin, that he then deduced that this -- that the description of the tail fin was that of the munition.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. And would you agree with me, sir, that the munition being unmarked and unpainted would seem to indicate that this round was newly manufactured rather than regular pre-war stock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't necessarily arrive at that deduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you expect that for regular or standard munitions one would find designations on it; it's either stamped or painted including batch, lot number, type of ordinance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can Mr. Ivetic specify whether he's talking about a munition before it has exploded or after it has exploded?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will then break up my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you expect a munition of this type, a mortar shell of 120 millimetres, before it has been exploded, to be painted and marked in such a way so as to identify the type of munition, the batch, et cetera, either by stamping or by painting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the practice in many armies, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you expect that such a munition, if so stamped and marked, if it was then utilised with the remnants of the ordinance, perhaps have but not necessarily the same markings visible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It might.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In this instance the gentleman upon whom you are relying says that the remnants of the mortar shell that caused this incident were unmarked; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what he put in his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was that your conclusion that you accepted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I accepted it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What can -- can you tell me about this report and does it apply to the other four rounds that fell as part of this incident? Were these munitions also recovered and were they similarly determined to be unmarked in the manner that this individual has identified of this particular munition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd have to read the report again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is there any reason why not to agree on whether this report covers all five or just four? I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There is. It's very critical to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but on whether it covered by the report? I mean, what you find in the report --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I see what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is there any reason why not you can agree with Mr. Groome, whether true or not, that what is found in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think the problem is with the report. We're talking about two reports. We are talking about this report that is contained within the comprehensive report that Mr. Baxter put together at the behest of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, your question was about this report and does it apply to the other four rounds, where I now understand that you are referring to another report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This report, does it apply to the other four rounds that fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, is there -- is it mentioned somewhere? I take it, then, it applies to the extent the other four rounds are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The other four rounds are mentioned in other portions of this comprehensive report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So therefore then you can agree with Mr. Groome that the other four rounds are mentioned somewhere else in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am asking for the witness to clarify with respect to this document, this sub-report that is on our screen, whether it applies. That's where I believe the confusion arises, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's where the confusion arises from. I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I could just ask you once again to clarify now, when we are dealing with this document that's up on the screens, this annex to the original report, do you know or did you take any steps to determine whether this analysis conducted by this French officer of sector Sarajevo applied to all of the munitions recovered from the site of the so-called Markale II incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't -- I'd need to read the whole report again and its covering document as to whether or not -- whether he is basing his latter paragraph on only the discovery of the one tail fin and whether that -- and which round that tail fin came from to answer that question. I -- I would certainly at this range of time from this incident, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, sir, did UNPROFOR have knowledge that both sides were manufacturing ordinance during wartime often at improvised factories for the use of their forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we suspected it rather than had knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. I will accept that. Could you please tell me, sir, if you know, what method was employed by this member of the engineering cell of sector Sarajevo to differentiate this unpainted and unmarked ordinance from any unpainted and unmarked ordinance produced and used by the Bosnian government forces so as to exclude the same from this analysis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know or would you agree with me, sir, that, in fact, this report by a Lieutenant-Colonel Mougey is operating backwards, starting with the assumption that the shell came from the Bosnian Serb positions, and thus merely examining whether this type of munition was used by the Serbs, not analysing comprehensively to determine without doubt the manufacturer of this particular round?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If it's asking whether -- for General Smith to speculate about what Lieutenant-Colonel Mougey was thinking about when he wrote this report, which I am not sure he was able to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you, please -- the question is, apart from speculation, is so composite, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's better to take it down in portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did this report, this examination, by lieutenant-colonel who was in a subordinate unit in sector Sarajevo, was it initiated by your command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the business of the -- the sector, wherever it was, to carry out an investigation of these incidents. So it was initiated by the incident and the sector headquarters would have reacted to it and sent the appropriate team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In including this sub-report by Lieutenant-Colonel -- it's either Mougey or Mougey -- in including it in the comprehensive report sent by your MA, Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter, was the intent of BH command to rely upon this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in its -- not only this report. We had the UNMO report and then I had a further investigation done in order to rationalise the two sets of reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you, prior to asking for the commencement of air strikes, take any steps to verify what method was used by this individual preparing this report which you intended to -- to rationalise with other reporting to reach a decision or to support a decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was satisfied that he was competent to make such an investigation, if that's what you mean by that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you take any steps to determine his competency or the methods used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was -- as I say, I was satisfied that he was competent. He's an engineer of a NATO army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We can now move to annex B of the comprehensive report offered by Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter. And I believe that's three pages later in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, does this appear to be a daily situation report from UNMO sector Sarajevo from the day of the incident, or a summation of -- of a sitrep summation of the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's such a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now we talked about your paragraph 198 of your statement, and you did -- you did clarify that you perhaps did know of -- of random shellings attributed to the ABiH forces. Looking through these pages of this annex we see various fire reports either increp or outgoing that are attributed to the ABiH forces. Would those be the type of incidents that you were referring to when you answered my previous question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could we turn the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. And would you agree with me that there are various entries that are identified as either originating from the ABiH positions or with the comments "fired ABiH"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at page 13 in the English and 14 in the B/C/S, and item number D of the same which starts at the bottom of the page in English and bleeds over onto the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you take a glance at that, sir, and would you confirm for me that, in fact, this appears to be a discussion of the Markale II incident which we have been examining?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is this in this comprehensive report?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We're still with that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could have the next page for the witness to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you could give me an indication of when you're ready to proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we can go.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now looking here, sir, would you agree with me that this UNMO report identifies that one mortar tail fin was recovered and that it had a batch marking of MK/M74/KB 93020?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's a 7, but otherwise yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. It is a 7 at the end. How would you explain the fact that the report by the French UNPROFOR engineer we just looked at said that the munition he recovered and reviewed was unmarked? Would you agree that there's a major discrepancy between these two investigations of the same incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If he's referring, we've only deduced that his comments about marking is about that tail fin. It doesn't actually say that. So I wouldn't make that complete -- that direct connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can refer to this UNMO report, it would seem to indicate that there was only one tail fin recovered or am I reading it incorrectly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the UNMO report says that the tail fin and it has that marking on, but as my memory of the document you first showed me, we the -- the comments about whether the thing is marked or not is not directly connected to the tail fin. We in discussion just now deduced that it might be. But since I'm not the author of the report and it's a along time ago, I can't be sure it's a connection we can make.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. Can we deduce from this UNMO report whether or not the remaining four rounds were recovered at the scene or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They'd exploded so they wouldn't have been recovered. Whether people picked up the bits and pieces that might be left, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 18 of this document in e-court in English and page 19 in the B/C/S. And first of all, we see the comment that the UNMOs are unable to confirm which WF fired the rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you assist us with this abbreviation? Is WF warring faction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where does it say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At the top of the page under "comment."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah, I see. I would expect that that's probably what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does this comment or conclusion by the UNMOs comport with your recollection of the UNMO position as to this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember their final position, but at the time everyone's trying to work it out, so what we think has happened, so it doesn't surprise me that in a report such as this they don't confirm one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look down at the item marked crater analysis, for item (a) we see a type of weapon identified as a 120-millimetre mortar, batch number MK M74KB9307; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I read there, yup.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now that is a completely different number than the number that was recorded at page 13 of this report, which had KB 93070?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not sure completely different is a fair characterisation of the number. Can the witness be shown both numbers so he isn't asked to try and recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure. I just gave him the number. But sure we can put up page 13 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it a different number? I apologise. The number from page 13 that we had just discussed had at the end KB 93070, as I recall. And as I recall you corrected me on that number. And this one has KB 9307. Was that a discrepancy that your office followed up on prior to engaging in air strikes against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just let me -- yes. One's got a "not" on the end and the other hasn't. That's what we're saying. So on the assumption that this is -- I don't think anybody was arguing about whether -- what the number was on the end. I can't remember that being raised at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you could take the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to find out, I see that under (a) we've got that MK M74KB9307. We have the same number under (b). Is this the same thing, or are these two different munitions if I may use the term that's been used?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If -- I think what you're reading here is the -- oh, hang on a minute. Just let me read again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I can assist, Your Honour, (b), (c) and (d) and (e) all have the same notation on the following -- on the next pages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah, this is each -- this is, as I understand this bit of the report is each specific crater, so there is a crater A, a crater B, a crater C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is this type of weapon with markings of MKM 74, is that a marking of some mortar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding of this is that this is the -- they are referring to the tail fin batch number on the mortar round as opposed to the mortar itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now the question I have for you sir that we've preluded to now, here, this report, for this portion of the UNMO report, this portion of your comprehensive report, now talks about all of the tail fins being recovered and all bearing these batch numbers which we have discussed. Did you note this discrepancy between now three parts of the same report and did you undertake any efforts to illuminate the matter before reaching a decision to ask for air strikes against the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a third set of reporting when I had my intelligence officer take both sets of reports and conduct his own survey of the situation, analysis of the situation, in that I cannot recall at this range. But it would be those -- I wanted to make sure that these two sets of reports had been compared with each other and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you've just identified your own intelligence officer. We've had evidence of multiple UNPROFOR witnesses at this trial that UNPROFOR did not have intelligence and did not gather intelligence. Could you clarify who you mean by your intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He -- it was by -- I've forgotten his nomenclature. S -- no, it's G, isn't? No, he's G2, an officer, which is an intelligence branch, and he was responsible for the information that we collected, which is -- I draw a distinction between the collection of intelligence by secret means.
