And he was the one that I asked to do this particular job for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I ask if that individual has a name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's in my statement. Colonel Powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to make sure we are talking about the same person. Now, am I correct that -- well, strike that. Here we have listed a bearing for the first shell of 170 degrees magnetic. We actually had testimony here the other day, at transcript page 7154 and 7169, including the videotape of the officers making the measurements wherein it was determined that it was 160 degrees. Do you know how and why your full comprehensive report now has this changed to 170 degrees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because -- I think you'll find that that's in one of the reports, and you've also got people using a different -- not degrees but mils, a different measure of arc.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was the decision made by your command to evade public scrutiny for this comprehensive report based upon the fact that there were these discrepancies which you could not explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We -- the purpose of the third investigation which I told you about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which discrepancies are you referring to at this moment, Mr. -- is it about the degrees and the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, the first report indicating one tail fin, unmarked. These -- the first UNMO report indicating one tail fin marked with a particular number. The third UNMO indicating four tail fins recovered each with marks and a different number than the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are still talking about the tail fins?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought we were talking about the bearings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the bearing I guess, now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's split that up. Let's clearly make a distinction between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's focus on the tail fins, sir. Was that a reason why your command wanted this report to be exempt from public scrutiny?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now let's talk about the differences in the degrees, although I believe your report is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I told you at the beginning of this bit of evidence the reason that I wanted it so that public scrutiny wasn't immediately -- we didn't start a -- so as to avoid starting a sort of argument in the media as to where people were being experts without actually being there on the ground and using partial bits of information that they were -- they were collecting off my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, had you been on the ground? Or were you also relying on partial bits of information in making your determination and seeking to turn the key to initiate air strikes against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a competent staff whose business -- and subordinates, whose business was to carry out these investigations on my behalf. I conducted -- they conducted two of them. I caused a third to be conducted and then arrived at a decision, which was my business to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, talk about the bearings. That's one of the inconsistencies you referred to. I think we had 2800 mils and we find in other documents 2.850 mils.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Here we find 170 plus or minus 5. May I take it that you have looked at tables what 2.800 mils exactly is in degrees?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The French standard is actually -- in this document it's identified as 2.850 for the French. As for the UNMOs, I'm not sure what their --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But my simple question is: What is 2.850 mils in degrees on a 360-degrees circle? I mean, that's -- if you are talking about inconsistencies, of course we have to carefully look at what the numbers exactly tell us. If you'll -- I'll find it for you if you -- that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the point is that these are all questions that experts would have to undertake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Ivetic. If you are talking about inconsistencies you first have to establish that there are inconsistencies. That's what we start with before we ask questions. The other question you would like to ask is: Why have you not changed -- okay, that's an interesting question, not the core of this case, why have you not expressed it in another numeric system as you did. And then I can imagine what the answer of the witness is: My experts used their own usual numbers. So for us it is to find out exactly whether there are inconsistencies. If they are there, we certainly have to pay attention to it. But if you say, I have not checked what 2.850 mils is in degrees or 2.800, then we'll do it over the break and then we'll have perhaps a better basis for any inconsistencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It depends on which standard of mils is being applied. The French use one, the British use one, the Soviets use another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we have to not only look at one system of mils but we have to look at the various system of mils which apply, as is done in other cases, and they we'll analyse all that and then see what the outcome is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is apply as is done in other cause case, and then we'll analyse all that and then see what the outcome is. I take it, Mr. Smith, are very familiar with the different systems in mils because they are not uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think with the possible exception of the Russians, those who use mils, it's a standard unit. There are 6.400 of them to a circle of which there are also 360 degrees, so it's roughly 17 mils to the degree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the mils system you're familiar with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe that is the one that was being used there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to annex C of this report which is the -- annex C of your comprehensive report which is the last page in e-court in both versions of this document. And this appears to be the third investigation that you indicated was conducted by Lieutenant-Colonel Brian Powers, a G2?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't believe the witness referred to it as a third investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There -- all right. Third.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How would you refer to this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What did I do in my initial statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why not focus on the document and then ask questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's third, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Third report. Let's look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It says at the beginning: "Following an investigation and analysis of all evidence ..." So now I have to ask you because the other side has raised this issue, was there a third investigation or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I called it a second iteration of this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Lieutenant-Colonel Brian E. Powers, your G2 investigation officer, am I correct that he was an American officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that he was an American intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall his branch that he came from. He was in the staff branch for intelligence in my headquarters, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is he the same Lieutenant-Colonel Powers that you identify in your book as being your link to NATO intelligence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, Lieutenant-Colonel Powers, can you tell me what, if any, experience he has in terms of artillery weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Why did you select him to do this second reiteration of investigation and analysis? Didn't you have trained artillery officers under your command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in my headquarters I didn't. I -- I can't remember why I chose him in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were there trained artillery officers in either your subordinate command or in your superior command, UN HG Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There might have been, but there weren't in my headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did Lieutenant-Colonel Powers perform any of the analysis as to bearings that were reflected in his report or was he merely relaying what others had determined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, at this distance I can't remember precisely how he conducted the report that -- conducted the investigation that led to this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me whether and which of the accepted methods of crater analyses were utilised either by Lieutenant-Colonel Powers or those he was relying upon for this report? Was it fuse furlough, centre of crater analysis, side-spray method, splinter-groove method or some other method?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember the precise details of the methodology used.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we look at the -- if we can turn back to the second page of this comprehensive report --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. It's page 2 in the English and also in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in item number 1, General, there is a reference to a written report about this incident having been given to him at 0800 hours, 29 August 1995. Would "him" refer to command UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It -- I read that as, yes, that I, commander UNPROFOR, received a written report at 8.00 on the 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall receiving a written report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as precisely as it's written there, but I'm sure I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I have not seen that written report specifically identified in this comprehensive report. Would it be one of the ones that we've gone through or would it be a report in addition to the three reports that we've gone through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page of this --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, am I correct that this part we are looking at now authored by Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter would be a summation of the supporting materials that we have now gone through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the page has just changed. I am not sure what I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is page 2 of the final and comprehensive report, authored 8 September --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree with me that Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter did not engage in any investigation, measurements or analysis, but was merely summarising what the source documents that we just went through reported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's my understanding of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we see here the Cymbeline radar is identified at number 4. Would you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that this is a British radar system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not on that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we go to next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I could direct your attention to number 4, the Cymbeline radar is identified. Am I correct that this was a British manufactured system originally known as field artillery 15 or number 15?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The unit is certainly British. What it was originally known as, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Am I correct that this system was first introduced in 1975 and already considered obsolete by most militaries who used the system as of 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if you're correct or not about what other people considered, and I don't know when it was introduced into service.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know what variant of the Cymbeline system was employed in Sarajevo in 1995? Was it the MK 1 or the MK 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I am looking at the clock. I think it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that'd be great, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I neglected to ask you earlier in regards to the comprehensive report that we've been looking at whether, in fact, anyone had performed any inquiry or investigation as to the marked tail fins, whether those batch number and origin markings correlated to any manufacturer within the arms system of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember if that had been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that if any of the teams that were employed by UNPROFOR at any time to investigate this incident took into account hand-held grenade launchers, such as the RBM-57 which could also have been utilised to fire rounds of that calibre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I -- I'm not familiar with the weapon in -- that you -- that you've given me a description of, and I don't know if they looked at other weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's then turn to what your report did use, and that would be the Cymbeline radar again. Do you recall, sir, irrespective of which model it was, the Cymbeline radar that was in place in Sarajevo and upon which your report relies, did it have the capability to record and playback data memory or was it one that had to be first-hand observed by the operator in situ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall what it's capabilities were in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct, sir, that for the functioning of the Cymbeline radar system, the -- in order for it to track and locate the source of a mortar fire position, that the operator would have to mark his screen at each bomb position and change the beam angle, and then it would have to place electronic markers against his marks representing the bomb's position on the horizontal plane such that operator intervention was required to track any projectiles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's been a very long time since I watched a Cymbeline operator at work, and I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I'll skip a few questions and ask you: Do you recall if at time-period of this incident there were actually three Cymbeline positions set up throughout Sarajevo, some operated by the British, some operated by the French?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember the deployment of the system, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was the system such that it covered all of Sarajevo or were there other gaps or holes in the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't -- I just can't recall that degree of detail at this distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the practice was for the Cymbeline radar operators to physically monitor the devices 24/7?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I can't remember how the -- that degree of detail of the -- how the operation was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. If we can turn to your statement, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, this would be P785, marked for identification. And page 52 in English, page 41 in the B/C/S. And -- I apologise, did I say the paragraph? No, paragraph 205.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And here, sir, is a reference to your first telephonic conversation or discussion with General Mladic after the occurrence of this incident known as Markale II, and I would direct your attention to the part that reads as follows. It's in the middle of the paragraph: "Mladic claimed that this was a Muslim attack designed to discredit the BSA. I had heard those claims before. And at the time I was in the theater at no stage had I ever been shown any evidence to support such an assertion." And the question I have for you: Am I understanding you correctly to say that you did not have any information tending to show that in prior instances Muslims had fired upon their own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that I had heard that the Muslims had attacked the Serbs and I had never been shown any evidence to support such an assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm misreading this, but I thought here you were talking about a Muslim attack against their own, against persons within Sarajevo. That was what Markale --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] My mistake. I'm -- I'm saying it wrong. That the Muslims had attacked themselves in order to discredit the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And my question -- and my question to you, sir, was to clarify these -- these things that you had heard about Muslims attacking themselves, were they in relation to other incidents, i.e., predating Markale, is what I'm asking you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. These had been -- this had been said on other occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to paragraph 202, which would be on the prior page in English, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here -- here you outline the factors or evidence that you relied upon to conclude that it must have been the Serbs who fired that round at Markale. Would your lack of -- of confirmed knowledge of prior instances where the Muslims were found to have fired on themselves also be included on this list as factors that convinced you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was dealing with this as a -- as -- otherwise why would I have done these -- this investigation for itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at the one part of this paragraph that reads: "And finally, it is my experience of being in a siege that rounds that fall on the inside of the siege tend to come from outside the siege."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you agree with me that this isn't really a method of proof, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, and that's perhaps why I put it as separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I put it to you, sir, although you've said that you have no -- you've heard claims made before but had not been shown any evidence to support such assertions, I'd like to put to you two factors that we have in evidence. We have two instances that occurred either during the time-period of your tenure or around the time-period of your tenure wherein there is strong indications that the Bosnian Muslim forces attacked their own. I'd like to ask if you've heard these. The first instance was the UN GOFRS personnel, John Jordan. He testified at transcript page 1.805 of this case of a July 1995 incident wherein his vehicle was targeted by BiH forces and his vehicle was perforated. Now, do you recall Mr. Jordan being in theater during the time-period that you were BH commander and did you hear of this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not immediately. Who was John Jordan?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He was the leader of the UN GOFRS fire-fighting squad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is a UN GOFRS?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: They were the volunteer fire-fighters operating in Sarajevo, putting out fires and helping assist the local fire department in performing their duties. They later became called the UN fire department, I believe. UN fire-fighting force.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you. Mr. Ivetic, this is what happens if you give a long story and then say, Do you know John Jordan? Shall we do it from the other side. First, try to find out what the witness knows. Because then the witness says, Who is it, what happened, et cetera. And then, of course, you are invited to again five the story. Try to find out what the witness knows about John Jordan or GOFRS or fire fighters, and then we hear from him and then we'll [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's go closer to home.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with David Fraser? At the time he was a major and now he's a general retired from the Canadian Armed Forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that he served as MA to the sector Sarajevo command, subordinate to you during the time-period that you were in theatre in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was there fairly early in the year, but I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you're developing a speed which really is --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- impossible to follow for -- even for listening it's not easy. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can perhaps assist you, sir. I believe he was in theater until May of 1995 as the MA of the sector Sarajevo commander. Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now we had testimony Mr. Fraser here at transcript page 5.880 through 5.881 of an incident wherein some mortar shells landed that were attributed to the Serbs and the BiH Muslim side fired additional mortar rounds at that same location which caused signature casualties amongst the Bosnian Muslim population who had come to view the results -- to view the prior shelling. And this was said to be confirmed by a UN investigation. Did you have knowledge of this incident that either predated your command or occurred during your command? I'm not saying that it did. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In -- was the Cymbeline radar system in place during the time-period prior to Markale; and if so, what time-period prior to Markale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in place prior to Markale II, and I think it was deployed after Markale I, but I am not absolutely sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In -- with respect to this incident that General Fraser discussed, there was no mention of Cymbeline. Would it be -- would it be -- would it be interesting for you to have analysed that to determine if those particular shells were also untracked by the Cymbeline radar system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I might say so, this is so hypothetical. I have no knowledge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- of the -- Mr. Fraser is -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, you don't have to answer that question. Mr. -- let's focus not on whether the witness would be interested to find out about a matter he has no knowledge about. Of course a curious person would have -- and whether a witness is a curious person, yes or no, is not the most important thing to hear today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's look at page -- paragraph 208 of your statement. It's in page 53 in the English and page 41 of the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I want to focus on what you said to General Mladic. And it says: "I informed him that it was now beyond reasonable doubt that the shells had come from BSA territory and the firing pointed had been 3.5 to 4 kilometres south-west of the impact point." Now I want to ask you, sir, where is this evidence that you represented was beyond a reasonable doubt as to the contents of the two paragraphs that we looked at? Are we talking about the comprehensive and full report that we have looked at? What is it that you are relying upon when you are making such a strong and bold assertion to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- the report that is summarised in that -- that you have been putting on the screen and the briefings that I'd had associated with it led me to form the -- the opinion, which was mine to form, the judgement was mine to make, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If -- and when you say the -- the opinion was yours to form, the judgement was yours to make, am I more correct that the decision to bomb was yours to make and that decision had already been made by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decision to bomb was -- had been made. It wasn't mine to make. The decision to request the bombing, to turn the key, was mine to make and that's what I subsequently did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look for a moment at document number 10231. This is dated the 18th of August -- pardon me, 28th of August, 1995, and is from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps command, signed by a Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Signed by a Colonel Sladoje. And in item 1 it states as follows: "1. I caution again all the unit commanders regarding my order on restricting fire at the city of Sarajevo without approval from the Corps Command Post."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree with me that based upon this document it would appear that prior to the incident at Markale that the VRS had banned fire upon the city of Sarajevo by its subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What am I to agree with?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Item number 1. Would you agree that this would seem to indicate that prior to the Markale incident there had been an order sent restricting fire on the city of Sarajevo without the approval of the commander corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's not the same as banned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The second way of summarising it was slightly different from the first time. Mr. Ivetic, you added now "without approval," and that is now answered by the witness. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And also Mr. Ivetic is saying that this order was before the -- the bombing. Can I ask what that's based on? Because there would seem to be some endorsements and this would suggest otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The text on paragraph number 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, may I take it that ... Yes, please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The item 1 which says: "I caution again all the unit commanders regarding my order on restricting fire at the city of Sarajevo without approval." That's what I'm basing it on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The "again" suggests that it was done earlier and the exact time of this was when Mr. -- when this document -- it's dated the 28th, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This comes after the incident, because you will see in the second part they are asking the units if anyone actually fired during the time-period of the incident --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- because this is what this document is seeking. So if you look at [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By 14 hours, and that means that this must be shortly before 1400 hours before this was issued. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can read the second part, sir, it says: "You are to inform the Corps Command, in writing, by 1400 hours, whether you have opened fire between 1000 and 1200 hours at Sarajevo. If you have, inform us when, the target of fire, which calibre and weapon was used and for what reason. The report is to be submitted for artillery weapons of calibre 80 millimetre and larger." Based upon the time being sought and the date of this order, would you agree that this would appear to be an inquiry to determine if any of their units might have shot at Sarajevo so as to be the source for the Markale II shell or shells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It looks as though that's what the initial -- the order is seeking to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And with respect to -- as an army officer, as a commander, would you consider this as a reasonable step if a military commander had not issued any orders for a fire mission to take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you consider this a -- he's trying -- yes. He's trying to find out what it is that's been going on. Yup.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you consider that this document corroborates what General Mladic told you on phone, that he was investigating whether any of his units had engaged in any action that could have resulted in the Markale incident, the Markale II incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His corps commander is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wish to tender this document at this time; however, now I see where the confusion arises. There appears to be an error in the translation into English. The B/C/S original says "zabrana," which would mean "zabrani otvarani vatra [phoen]," which hopefully can get translated. And I'll say it again, "nardzeni o zabrani otvarani vatra [phoen]," [Interpretation] "order on prohibition to open fire." [In English] So it's a little bit stronger than just a restriction. But, Your Honours, with that in mind, I would tender this document as the next available exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 10231 shall be assigned Exhibit D137, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. It is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to take a look at one more document and ask a question or two about that in the time that we have left. If we can call up 1D00596 and call up page 9 in e-court. This should correlate to a page from the Karadzic transcript of T 11485, and I would like to focus on lines 14 through 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for that -- well, we'll just wait for that. I will be brief with it. And it reads as follows: "Q. While we are waiting for this to appear on the screen, General, in the first week of May, you said, and you repeated it in your statement and we shall come back to it, that you were under great pressure that a bombing should take place. Who was exerting this pressure? "A. There was pressure from the NATO authorities, who were watching the circumstances in and around the exclusion zones. There were demands from the Bosnian government in addition." Now this is in relation to the time-period in May of 1995. First of all, do you affirm the truthfulness and accuracy of this answer that you gave in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The question I want to ask you is -- again, this was dealing with May 1995: Can we conclude that pressure from the same bodies, that is to say, from the NATO authorities and the Bosnian government, was ever present and perhaps increased in August of 1995 when this Markale II incident was being discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The circumstances by the end of August were quite different to those in May, and I don't recall the -- the -- let me answer it slightly different: As a result of the London Conference and the decisions made there and announced then, the sense -- my sense of this discord between NATO and the UN positions had much decreased.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One more question and then we can break for the day, if I can, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very short one because we are already beyond quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did pressure from NATO and the Bosnian government have any role in your decision to employ NATO aircraft and your Rapid Reaction Force in August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we can have the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. We will adjourn for the day, Mr. Smith, and we'd like to continue Monday morning at 9.30. Were you able to arrange for your presence on Monday? I do understand that you'd very much like to finish on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I -- I will be here on Monday, always assuming the trains are running to schedule. What I'm -- I have also -- it may help the Court to know that I have been able to call London --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have dealt with that in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But for this moment, so you'll be available on Monday morning. It seems that Mr. Mladic seeks either to contact with counsel. If he wants to writes a little note, of course, we'll wait with adjourning until he has written it. Mr. Smith, we briefly do turn into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Therefore we'll -- we'd like to see you back on Monday. And apart from the discussions we just referred to, you're hereby again instructed not to speak with anyone about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given, and we'd like to see you back on the 28th at 9.30 in the morning. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is no urgent matter to be raised at this moment we'll adjourn for the day and will resume Monday, the 28th of January, at 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 28th day of January, 2013, at 9.30 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.18 p.m.,
